name: Islamic modernism
summary: Islamic modernism is the 19th and 20th century reform current that tries to reconcile Islamic faith with modern science, constitutional government and education. It rejects blind imitation (taqlid) in favour of renewed independent reasoning (ijtihad) and treats sharia as adaptable through public interest (maslahah) and the higher aims of the law. It is anti-colonial but admires Western institutions, and stays distinct from secularism by keeping faith in public life.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Ameer Ali says animal life stands on the same footing as human life in the sight of the Creator and praises the Prophet's teaching of kindness to animals.

ban-interest.rationale: Abduh as mufti permitted accepting interest on loans; Ameer Ali says the Prophet banned riba but not legitimate profit on loans for trade.

change-traditions-that-no-longer-suit.rationale: Modernists separate basic commands from contingent rules given for their time and place, liable to amendment as circumstances change.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Split inside the movement: modernists tended to accommodate foreign rulers and sometimes accepted their civilizing mission, while Afghani held strong anti-imperialist feelings.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Iqbal rejected materialist socialism and the modernist tradition does not see class conflict as history's driver.

clerical-rule.rationale: Iqbal wanted the ulema to be a part of a legislative assembly, not hold supreme authority; Rida after 1905 shifted toward ulema leadership so some dissent.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Kemal holds that the sultan's right is to govern on the will of the people and the principles of freedom; Gale: he read shura and bay'a as parliament and popular sovereignty.

dominated-front.rationale: Split: Afghani sought to unite Muslim rulers against European domination (pan-Islam), but Gale says many modernists accommodated their foreign rulers and Abduh preached cooperation with Britain.

elective-rulers.rationale: Split: Iqbal approves an elected Assembly as caliph and says the republican form is consistent with Islam, while the Young Ottomans held to constitutional monarchy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Ameer Ali says Islam made men equal in the eye of the law; the statement is about all people and he writes mainly of Muslims and subjects within Muslim states.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Iqbal says Islam is neither nationalism nor imperialism and treats racial distinctions as only for reference.

initiating-nondefensive-force-unjustifie.rationale: Modernists rejected aggressive war as non-liberal (Gale on Khan) and Ameer Ali describes Islamic war as self-defence only; neither addresses force outside war, so +1 not +2.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The movement argues for the compatibility of Islam with Western rationality, science, progress, constitutionalism; Kurzman presents it as the counterexample to a permanent clash between Islam and the West.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Iqbal holds that the Qur'an gave simple legal principles to be developed by interpretation and by a Muslim legislative assembly; Gale: modernists put the egalitarian spirit of the Qur'an above later rulings.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Iqbal denied that material forces alone decide, and rejected atheistic socialism; modernists treat ideas and spirit as central.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The Young Ottomans held an ideology of constitutional monarchy and Tahtawi looked to cooperation between an enlightened monarch and progressive ulama; Iqbal's republican view is a counterpoint, but the monarch stays acceptable.

more-religion-public.rationale: Split: Iqbal rejects the separation of church and state (the spiritual and temporal are not distinct domains in Islam), while Gale says modernists distrust Islamist politics and do not collapse religious discourse into political legitimacy.

one-spouse-at-a-time.rationale: Ameer Ali argues the Koranic condition on plural wives amounted in reality to a prohibition of polygamy and that the state may abolish it.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Iqbal welcomed legislative assemblies taking over ijtihad as modern ijma, giving them lawmaking authority.

party-controls-media.rationale: Khayr al-Din held that integration into the modern world meant responsible parliamentary government and freedom of the person and the press.

patriotic-education.rationale: Split: Tahtawi wanted universal schooling to inculcate patriotic feelings, while Iqbal describes patriotism and nationalism as a new loyalty that narrows thought and sets Islam against nationalism.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Modernists made constitutionalism a guarantee of civil rights and freedoms; Ameer Ali stresses an executive subordinate to law and equality in the eye of the law.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Iqbal says Islam is neither nationalism nor imperialism but a League of Nations that treats racial distinctions as reference only and not as a basis for restriction.

racial-pride.rationale: Iqbal says Islam recognizes racial distinctions for facility of reference only, not for restricting the social horizon of its members.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Modernists reconcile reason with faith rather than rank reason as the only guide; Iqbal criticised pure intellect.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Core of the movement: scripture is continuously reinterpreted with reason and science as the measure, by ijtihad open to all Muslims, with contingent social and political rules amendable to changing circumstances.

religion-illusion.rationale: Iqbal's lectures argue religion is a real insight into reality and criticise materialism, and the movement rejects the claim.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Azad held that all faiths are one in their essence; Ameer Ali says the Koran does not confine salvation to the followers of Muhammad.

religious-nation.rationale: Documented split in India: Iqbal's supporters backed the Muslim League and Pakistan, Azad backed Congress and a unified Indian nation with universal humanism.

religious-offensive-war.rationale: Ameer Ali holds that Islam took up the sword only in self-defence and that proselytism by the sword was wholly contrary to the Prophet's instincts; Gale says modernists rejected aggressive war.

restore-past-order.rationale: Iqbal and Abduh criticised stagnation and taqlid and sought progress through reconstruction, not restoration.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Iqbal accepted republican, elected rule, and the modernist tradition rejects sacralised rulers.

separate-church-state.rationale: Iqbal states that in Islam church and state are one reality seen from two views and rejects the separation as a bifurcation; the Wikipedia article stresses modernism differs from secularism.

separated-powers.rationale: Ameer Ali says the body of jurisconsults served as a constitutional check on the sovereign and the executive stood under the law; presented approvingly, not as a worked scheme of separated powers.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Kemal says the religion of Muhammad rejects the sultan's claim to own the state; Ameer Ali says Islam made the executive subordinate to the law.

spiritual-nature.rationale: The modernists keep faith in public life, and Iqbal's Reconstruction treats religion as bearing on both spirit and the whole of life.

universal-morality.rationale: Iqbal and Abduh claimed reason and revelation are consistent and universal truths knowable by both.

vanguard-party.rationale: Iqbal rejected atheistic socialism; modernists are reformist.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Ameer Ali says the Prophet gave women the right to obtain a separation on reasonable grounds; he does not discuss divorce with no ground.

women-must-cover.rationale: Ameer Ali says the Koran gives no warrant for seclusion of women and that enjoining it is opposed to the spirit of the Prophet's reforms; he allows modest dress and privacy as advice, not law.

workers-councils.rationale: Iqbal rejected atheistic socialism; modernists favoured parliaments.

scope: Islamic modernism is the reform current that arose among Muslim scholars, officials and writers from the 1830s to the 1940s (Tahtawi, Khayr al-Din, the Young Ottomans such as Namik Kemal, Afghani and Abduh, Sayyid Ahmad Khan, Ameer Ali, Qasim Amin, Iqbal, Azad and the Russian Jadids), and that continues in later thinkers such as Fazlur Rahman. It holds that Islam agrees with reason, science, constitutional government and education, re-reads scripture through ijtihad instead of imitating past jurists, and separates what the faith commands from the social rules fitted to one time and place. Its core is the reconciliation of Islamic faith with modern institutions and ideals; the Salafi revival in Rida's later work, secular nationalism, Islamist movements and scholarship on other topics (colonial history, Muslim law in general) are outside it, except where they state modernists' own positions.
